aiOverview.content: A naturalized citizen in the United States is a foreign national who voluntarily becomes a U.S. citizen after fulfilling legal requirements established by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). Naturalized citizens hold the same rights, privileges, and responsibilities as native-born citizens, including the right to vote, hold public office (except for President and Vice President), and obtain a U.S. passport. As of 2024, approximately 26 million naturalized U.S. citizens lived in the United States, making up about 51% of the total foreign-born population. General Requirements for Naturalization (Form N-400) To be eligible for naturalization, an applicant must generally meet the following criteria: Age: Be at least 18 years old at the time of filing. Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR): Be a "Green Card" holder. Residence: Generally, five years of continuous residence as an LPR (or three years if married to a U.S. citizen). Physical Presence: Be physically present in the U.S. for at least 30 months out of the five years (or 18 months out of three years for spouses of citizens). Good Moral Character: Demonstrate good moral character for at least five years before applying (e.g., no serious criminal record). English & Civics: Be able to read, write, and speak basic English and pass a U.S. history and government test. Oath of Allegiance: Take an oath of allegiance to the United States. The Naturalization Process Application: File Form N-400, Application for Naturalization, with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Biometrics: Undergo fingerprinting and background checks. Interview/Test: Complete an interview with a USCIS officer and pass the English and civics tests. Oath of Allegiance: Take the oath in a ceremony to finalize the process. Recent Updates (2025-2026): New Civics Test: As of October 20, 2025, applicants must take a new 2025 naturalization civics test (20 questions; 12 correct to pass). Neighborhood Investigations: In August 2025, USCIS announced it would resume "neighborhood investigations" (personal investigations) for applicants, which may include requesting testimonials from neighbors or employers. Good Moral Character Guidance: Updated policy in 2025 directs officers to weigh positive attributes (community involvement, employment) alongside the absence of misconduct. Special Cases Military Personnel: Noncitizens serving in the U.S. Armed Forces may be exempt from residence and physical presence requirements, and may not have to be LPRs if serving during designated periods of conflict. Children: Children under 18 may automatically derive citizenship through their naturalized parents. Denaturalization A naturalized citizen's citizenship can be revoked (denaturalization) if it was illegally procured, such as by concealing material facts or willful misrepresentation during the process. This is a rare, high-stakes process usually handled by federal courts, and recent Department of Justice guidance has identified this as an enforcement priority.
